title: Struct-driven deserializers and stream-safety patterns for Go SDK
creator: Maya Chen
description: Problem: The current Go SDK surface for streaming responses relies on ad-hoc JSON envelope parsing and map[string]any glue in many examples. Consumers want a clear, typed, and memory-safe path for decoding streaming outputs into domain structs while preserving backpressure and retry semantics. This ticket adds a set of struct-driven deserializers, a small generics-based helper layer, and patterns for safe decoding when chunks split object boundaries or include partial tokens.
background: Related work (see existing tickets): teams have implemented many variations of streaming decoders (adapters, envelope mappers, streaming schema factories) but we still see confusion in internal examples and a recurring class of bugs: (1) panics when a streaming chunk splits a JSON object, (2) silent data loss when a decoder drops an unknown field, (3) excessive allocations when callers allocate intermediate maps per token. This has led to support tickets and inconsistent docs.
proposed_solution: Deliver a small public package internal/stream/typed that exposes: 1) A Decoder[T any] type that consumes io.Reader/byte slices and yields (T, error) items as they are completed, handling partial-chunk buffering and incremental JSON parsing. 2) A lightweight envelope annotation via struct tags (redwood:\"json_envelope:response\") to map nested streaming envelopes into typed fields without reflection-heavy cost. 3) Retry-safe resume token semantics: decoder can persist and restore a minimal parse state so retries from the server can resume without duplicating items. 4) Examples: a chat-stream example that yields ChatDelta structs, and an embeddings-stream example that streams EmbeddingVector structs. 5) Unit tests for edge cases: object-split, concatenated-objects, interleaved-non-json-heartbeats. 6) Micro-benchmarks comparing allocations and throughput vs current ad-hoc approach.
design_decisions:
- Use encoding/json's Decoder with a small incremental buffer for correctness, but provide a fast-path that uses ffjson-like raw-to-struct when chunk boundaries align.
- Avoid large reflection on hot paths by requiring generated or explicitly-specified typed constructors when zero-allocation performance is requested.
- Keep API ergonomic: Decoder[T] implements Next(ctx) (returns (T, error)) and Close().
- Persistence of parse state will be limited to buffer position + last-complete-object-offset to keep resume implementation simple and auditable.
risks:
- Complexity of maintaining parse-state across heterogeneous servers (different envelope framing). Mitigation: limit resume to our canonical streaming envelopes and fall back to client-side de-duplication for unknown framing.
- Performance regressions if reflection-heavy code is accidentally used. Mitigation: add CI micro-bench thresholds and review.
- API surface might leak internals; mitigation: expose only a stable minimal surface and keep helpers internal if necessary.
acceptance_criteria: Decoder[T] implemented and exported in package internal/stream/typed
Three end-to-end examples added under sdk/go/examples/streaming: chat, embeddings, rerank
Unit tests covering chunk-splitting, concatenated objects, and heartbeat frames with >= 95% line coverage for the package
Benchmark showing <= 2x allocations vs current map-based approach for typical chat traces (measured on ci/bench)
Docs and README with migration guide and example usage added to the SDK docs site
Design doc and API review completed with @Anika Patel and @Jon Ruiz
